newsitem.title: USA: Lack of skilled workers widens trade deficit.
newsitem.headline: Lack of skilled workers widens trade deficit.

text.p: Many Americans have no idea why the United States has an unfavourable balance of trade, and what, if anything, they can do about it.
Why did we import $187 billion more of manufactured goods last year than we exported?

One explanation comes from Harry Moser, president of Charmilles Technologies Corp., Lincolnshire, Ill., one of the world's largest machine tool producers, and a man who is determined to do something about it.

It's not necessarily because foreigners work cheaper, either, he said. Thirteen countries pay their industrial workers more than U.S. employers pay. It's because they have the skilled workers and we don't.
"If we don't train Jack as a beautician, my wife will get her hair done by Jill instead of Jack," Moser said. "But it will get done in America because she can't go to Asia to get it fixed.
"But if we don't train John here to make a mould (used in manufacturing), the work will go to China and the wealth generated by that mould is lost," he said.

"Pretty soon China is using the mould to make parts, then they're designing and assembling parts and finished goods. You see a lot of computers, components, and household goods coming here from Asia," Moser noted.

"We've lost hundreds of millions of dollars a year just in tooling work because of this shortage of skilled labour," he said. And each manufacturing job that goes down the drain takes three to five support jobs with it.

So Moser is beating the drums to call attention to the tens of thousands of unfilled jobs that would pay $15 to $20 an hour to journeymen at 15,000 tool-making companies -- if they could only find such workers.

James Wallbeoff, educational consultant for the National Tooling & Machining Association, Ft. Washington, Md., puts the number of unfilled job openings for machinists and related occupations at 60,000.
Moser has personally distributed 30,000 fliers, mainly to young people, pointing out that machinists earn $40,000 to $60,000 a year and enjoy good job security.
"Those figures don't include those who become shop managers, go into sales or start their own shops," Moser said. Many apprentices will star as tomorrow's entrepreneurs, he said.

Among the fastest-growing businesses today, according to Cognetics Inc., a Cambridge, Mass., research firm, are small manufacturing "gazelles." And Michigan Future, of Ann Arbor, claims the state's best-paying new jobs are in manufacturing.

Young people, writes Stanley Modic, editor-in-chief of "Tooling & Production" magazine, Solon, Ohio, "avoid manufacturing careers like the plague" because when they think "machinist" it conjurs up outworn images of "dirty finger nails, oil-stained clothes, and dingy working conditions." That era, though, is long gone, Modic said.

Moser wants more high school students to become apprentice toolmakers. That would provide what he terms "true learning," reminiscent of a Chinese proverb he likes to quote: "I hear and I forget. I see and I remember. I do and I understand."

Unfortunately, just five out of 229 young apprentices surveyed during the 1995-96 school term by the Tooling & Manufacturing Association (NTMA) in Park Ridge, Ill., said they got the idea from high school guidance counsellors. Most apprenticed on the advice of family or friends.
The public schools must do more to interest students in technical jobs, Moser said. He also wants industrialists to arrange more student tours of their plants.

Filling industrial jobs, Moser believes, will do much to stop the decline of U.S. manufacturing and reduce the trade deficit. As matters stand, said Cornell University manufacturing authority Joseph Thomas, "Lots of manufacturing companies expect the skills problem to get worse."
The NTMA has some 50 chapters that arrange for on-the-job training for apprentices. For more information, call the group's hot line at 301-248-6200.
Information is also available from Charmilles Technologies, 560 Bond St., Lincolnshire, IL, 60069.
(EDITORS: Sherwood Ross is a freelance writer who covers workplace issues for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Ross.)
